verdict: OK to lend in Kollam coir, but only to working-capital borrowers with clean stock and domestic offtake; skip anyone carrying slow-moving mat inventory or export-dependent receivables.
title: Kollam coir products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Coir is a husk-to-cash conversion trade: buy coconut husk, ret fibre and pith, sell into mats, yarn, cocopeat and pith blocks.** Kerala produces 60 percent of world supply of white fibre [3], so Kollam's raw-material access is a genuine local advantage. Cash sits in two places: husk and fibre stock at the yard, and finished goods waiting for a buyer. **The sector's problem is not fibre supply, it is the speed at which finished stock converts to cash.**

## What has broken now
**Kerala State Coir Corporation is holding nearly ₹30 crore of coir products unsold for years, and the state is now clearing it through local-body kiosks at discounts up to 50 percent [1].** That is a direct price signal: discounted mat stock is about to hit the same domestic buyers your borrowers sell to. Delayed payments have already disrupted fund flow to cooperatives and societies, making wage commitments hard [1]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's own finished-goods ageing is stretching; if mats are older than a season, ask what price they expect to realise against the discounted kiosk stock [1].**

## Where the growth is
**Lend to the input side and the domestic consumable side, not to mat inventory.** Cocopeat and pith blocks move faster and are less exposed to the discount overhang; the kiosk network is also meant to support coconut-husk collection [1], which helps husk suppliers and small retters. **Pursue husk aggregators, cocopeat/pith processors and small retters selling into domestic institutional buyers; avoid borrowers whose book is long-dated mat stock or whose receivables sit with government-backed institutions already showing delayed payments [1].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure as short-tenor working capital against stock and receivables, with monthly stock-and-receivable statements as the price of the limit.** Take ageing of finished goods every month, husk purchase register every month, and quarterly GST returns to confirm turnover is real. **Kerala GST collections are running 10.3 percent Apr-to-date against India's 6.1 percent [D], so a borrower whose declared turnover lags that local trend needs explaining.** Keep term debt out unless it is for husk-yard or drying capacity with visible throughput.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for finished-goods days rising while sales stay flat, discount-led billing, and wage delays at the unit.** If a borrower starts selling mats at deep discount to match the kiosk clearance [1], treat it as a margin event, not a sales event. **Sources say little specific about Kollam city itself; the ₹30 crore stock figure is state-level [1], so lean on the borrower's own stock and receivable data rather than the headline.**
watch: Ageing crosses one season -> cut limit and ask for a clearance plan
Declared turnover grows slower than the 10.3% state trend [D] -> ask for sales register and buyer list
Payment delay beyond agreed terms -> shift to cash/advance billing or reduce exposure
Purchase volumes fall while sales hold -> check for stock substitution or unrecorded sales
Discounts approach the 50% kiosk clearance level [1] -> reprice limit and reassess margin
